newsitem.title: UK: Britain turns focus on drought, water supplies.
newsitem.headline: Britain turns focus on drought, water supplies.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government has called in water industry chiefs for an emergency conference on Monday to tackle the worst drought the country has faced in 200 years.
Britain, belying its traditional image of a land of heavy rain, is suffering its second dry year in a row, with eastern and southern parts of the country worst affected.

Labour, which swept to power in a landslide election victory on May 1, has been fiercely critical of the water companies since they were privatised at the turn of the decade by the previous Conservative government.

It has expressed outrage at the huge amount of water that leaks out of pipes -- estimated by some at 800 million gallons (3.64 billion litres) a day -- while companies pay out hefty dividends to shareholders and fat pay packets to executives.
Monday's meeting in London will bring together water companies, regulators and environmental and consumer lobby groups to discuss water resource problems.

"This government is determined to take decisive action to tackle the causes of the problems which the experience of the past few years and the current drought has highlighted," Deputy Prime Minister John Prescott said in a statement.

The Water Services Association, which represents many of the country's water and sewerage firms, welcomed the conference and said the industry was "keen to debate" how to achieve a sensible balance on supply and demand management along with environmental considerations.
The industry maintains that it has invested over 500 million pounds ($820 million) on drought-related measures and has under way "the biggest attack on leakage in its history".
It claims to have cut leakage by over 100 million gallons a day since the drought started in 1995.

But tackling leakage alone is unlikely to solve the problems of water shortage, which have brought some areas close to cutting essential domestic supplies and forced many consumers to endure bans on watering their gardens.

Customers are increasingly being targeted to trim demand and to treat water as a precious resource, through measures such as metering or higher tariffs for non-essential use in gardens and swimming pools.
"We want to see the companies getting together more with customers... everyone involved can develop their own ways of saving water," a spokesman for the environment department said.
The Water Services Association said the industry was trying to encourage customers "to use water wisely, in the home, in the garden and in the work place".
But it says new reservoirs might still be needed in some parts of the country and there could be calls to take extra water supplies out of rivers, a process known as "abstraction."
Environmental groups believe these measures are extreme and should be considered only as a last resort.
The conference will also look at the possibility that Britain's weather has undergone a radical change.
"Climate change and household growth are likely to put increasing pressure on water use. We need to take action now to ensure that everyone is playing their full part," Prescott said.
The Water Services Association warned that if lower rainfall becomes the norm, "the industry does not have the security of supply it would wish to have".
The government is hoping that the conference will be "a first step to start some action", the environment department spokesman said. ($= 0.609 British Pounds)
